title: Safe Patient Transfer (Bed to Chair / Wheelchair)
summary: Safely transferring a patient from bed to chair using proper body mechanics and assistive devices.
equipment: Chair or wheelchair with brakes locked
Lift device if needed (Hoyer lift for non-weight-bearing)
steps: Assess patient: strength, balance, weight-bearing status, fall risk, cognitive ability, previous transfer method.
Explain procedure to patient. Obtain assistance if needed (weight-bearing capacity guides number of staff).
Raise bed to chair-height. Lock bed wheels and chair wheels.
Assist patient to sit at edge of bed (dangle): place non-dominant arm behind shoulders, dominant arm under knees, pivot and swing to sitting. Allow 1–2 minutes to assess for orthostatic hypotension.
Apply gait belt snugly at waist (2 fingers fit). Have patient put on non-slip footwear.
Position chair at 45° angle to the bed on the patient's stronger side.
Instruct patient: lean forward, push up with arms, stand. Nurse grasps the gait belt (not the arms or shoulders).
Once standing: patient pivots toward chair. Nurse guides with gait belt.
Instruct patient to back up to chair until they feel it behind the knees, then slowly lower using arms.
Ensure patient is positioned correctly in chair. Ensure call light within reach.
safetyTips: NEVER transfer a patient alone if they are a fall risk or have limited strength without proper assistance or a lift device.
Gait belt on the WAIST — not under the axilla. Lifting under the arms causes shoulder injury.
Orthostatic hypotension: allow dangling time before standing. Monitor for dizziness and BP drop.

title: Assisted Ambulation (with Assistive Devices)
summary: Assisting a patient with ambulation safely, using gait belt and appropriate assistive devices.
equipment: Walker, cane, or crutches as appropriate
IV pole with wheels if needed
steps: Assess: fall risk score, pain, balance, endurance, weight-bearing restrictions, orthostasis history.
Verify physical therapy orders or weight-bearing restrictions.
Apply gait belt. Ensure patient has non-slip footwear.
Assist patient to standing (per transfer procedure). Pause 1–2 minutes — assess for dizziness, pallor.
WALKER: patient pushes walker forward, steps into it. Repeat. Walker should be at wrist height with elbows slightly flexed.
CANE: cane in hand opposite the weak/injured side. Advance cane, then weak leg, then strong leg (cane-weak-strong).
NURSE POSITION: stand at patient's weaker side and slightly behind. Hold gait belt with both hands.
Encourage patient to look up and ahead — not at their feet.
Observe gait: steadiness, steps, stride length, use of device.
IF PATIENT BEGINS TO FALL: do not try to hold them up. Guide the fall: lean patient into you, bend knees, lower them to the ground. Protect the head.
After ambulation: assist to chair or bed. Assess pain, tolerance, vital signs if indicated.
safetyTips: If a patient is falling, guiding a controlled fall is safer than trying to catch them — prevents injury to both patient and nurse.
First ambulation post-surgery or immobility: two staff minimum. High fall risk.
Orthostatic hypotension is common in hospitalized patients — always dangle before standing.
keyTakeaways: Cane on strong side, advance with weak leg first
Guide a fall — don't try to stop it

title: Passive Range of Motion (PROM) Exercises
summary: Performing passive range of motion to maintain joint mobility in dependent or immobile patients.
steps: Verify PT/provider orders or nursing protocol for PROM. Assess for contraindications: unstable fractures, joint dislocations, severe pain, recent joint surgery, deep vein thrombosis.
Explain procedure to patient. Assess pain level before starting.
Perform in a smooth, controlled, rhythmic manner — NO jerking or forced movement.
Support the joint above and below during each movement.
Neck: flexion, extension, rotation (NOT in trauma/cervical spine precautions).
Shoulder: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, internal/external rotation, circumduction.
Elbow: flexion/extension, supination/pronation.
Wrist: flexion/extension, radial/ulnar deviation.
Fingers: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction.
Hip: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, internal/external rotation.
Knee: flexion/extension.
Ankle: dorsiflexion/plantar flexion, inversion/eversion (prevents foot drop).
Perform each movement 5–10 times per joint. Stop if patient reports pain.
Document: joints exercised, patient tolerance, ROM limitations noted.
safetyTips: Stop immediately if you feel a click, crepitus, or patient reports sudden pain.
PROM does not build strength — it maintains joint mobility and prevents contractures.
Suspected DVT in a limb: DO NOT perform PROM on that extremity until cleared.
keyTakeaways: Support above and below the joint

title: Prone Positioning (ARDS / Acute Lung Injury)
summary: Positioning a critically ill ventilated patient prone to improve oxygenation in severe ARDS.
equipment: Prone positioning device or rolled blankets
Specialty face cradle or face pillow
steps: Indications: PaO2/FiO2 ratio <150 on FiO2 ≥0.6 and PEEP ≥5 for >12h (severe ARDS).
Pre-proning checklist: secure all lines/tubes (ETT, NG, IV lines, catheters). Note ETT cm mark.
Pre-oxygenate to 100% FiO2 for 2–5 minutes before turning.
Assign roles: one person per extremity + one for head and airway.
TURN: log roll to side, then onto prone in one coordinated movement called by the airway nurse.
Head: place in padded face cradle or turn to one side (alternate direction every 2h).
Chest rolls/positioning pillows: support under clavicles and ASIS to free the abdomen for diaphragmatic movement.
Arms: either in swimmer's position or at sides — pad elbows, knees, toes.
Eyes: closed and protected (corneal exposure risk). Check after turning.
Verify ETT position immediately after turn. Auscultate bilateral breath sounds.
Prone session: minimum 16 hours per session per evidence (PROSEVA trial).
Monitor: oxygenation, ETT security, skin under pressure points, facial edema.
safetyTips: Airway displacement is the most critical risk — airway nurse never leaves the head during the turn.
Facial edema develops rapidly in prone — corneal exposure can cause vision loss. Check eyes frequently.
Prone is contraindicated in: spinal instability, open abdomen, increased ICP, hemodynamic instability.
documentation: Prone start time and end time

title: Turning & Repositioning Schedule (Pressure Injury Prevention)
summary: Implementing a systematic turning and repositioning schedule to prevent pressure injuries in at-risk patients.
steps: Assess Braden Scale at admission and daily: score ≤14 = high risk for pressure injury.
Standard repositioning: q2h for bed-bound patients, q1h for those at very high risk.
Turn sequence: supine → right lateral (30° tilt) → supine → left lateral (30° tilt).
30° lateral tilt (NOT 90° side-lying): distributes weight over greater trochanter — avoids direct pressure on hip.
Inspect skin at EVERY repositioning: heels, sacrum/coccyx, trochanters, occiput, scapulae, elbows, ankles, medial knees.
HEELS: suspend heels off the mattress using heel protector boots or pillows under the calves. Never rest heels directly on the mattress.
Document repositioning times, position used, and skin findings.
Use pressure redistribution surface (foam overlay, low-air-loss mattress) for all high-risk patients.
Apply moisturizer to dry skin. Apply barrier cream to skin exposed to moisture (incontinence).
Patient education: shift weight q15 min if capable of chair sitting.
safetyTips: Heels are the second most common pressure injury site. Suspension is the only reliable prevention.
A 30° tilt (not 90°) avoids direct trochanter pressure — use wedge pillow to maintain position.
Repositioning alone is insufficient for very high-risk patients — combine with pressure redistribution mattress.
keyTakeaways: Heels must be suspended off the mattress
